meta.headline: **Partial implementation (B)** is the dominant outcome, and Suriname gives a detailed National Report: it acceded to the Convention against Torture (16 November 2021) and abolished the death penalty in its Military Criminal Code (2021, **A**), adopted the Equal Treatment in Employment Act and the Act on Violence and Sexual Harassment in Employment (2022), the Children's Ombudsperson Act (2025), a National Social Protection Strategy 2024-2030, a National Education Policy Plan 2024-2031, a Multilingual Education Programme, a National Policy Plan for Persons with Disabilities 2025-2030, a national FPIC protocol (2025) and a Land Rights Project, and introduced the General Act for Persons with Disabilities in Parliament. **No relevant action (C)** persists on the remaining optional protocols (OP-CAT, OP-CEDAW, OP-CRPD, OP-ICESCR, the Second Optional Protocol), ICPPED, the national human rights institution (draft Act only), legislation on sexual orientation and gender identity, the minimum age of marriage, corporal punishment, child labour, a standing invitation to special procedures and the Collective Rights of Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Act (still a draft).

themes.theme: Ratification of & accession to international instruments

Ratify the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment and its Optional Protocol

Complete the ratification of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (Malawi); Complete the process of ratifying the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, which is at an advanced stage as highlighted in the national report (Morocco); Finalize the process of ratifying the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment

Ratify the main international treaties on human rights that are still pending so as to move towards achievement of Sustainable Development Goals 5, 10 and 16
Prioritize the parliamentary debates necessary for the consideration of the ratification of the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance

recommendations.by: Costa Rica; Armenia; Australia; Iceland; Mexico; Portugal; Finland; France

recommendations.text: Ratify the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance and accept the competence of the Committee on Enforced Disappearances
Consider ratifying the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance

blocks.summary: Ratify OP-CEDAW
blocks.rationale: Ratification is in the pre-parliamentary preparatory phase.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 9 — Suriname: "Ratification of OPCAT, OP-CEDAW and OP-CRPD is currently in the preparliamentary preparatory phase"

recommendations.text: Ratify the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women

Ratify the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women and the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on a communications procedure

blocks.rationale: UNESCO recommends ratification; none is reported.

Consider ratification of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization Convention against Discrimination in Education

recommendations.text: Ratify the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women

blocks.summary: Ratify OP-CAT

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 3 — Human Rights Committee: "recommended that Suriname consider ratifying the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture"

recommendations.text: Proceed to ratify the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment

blocks.summary: Request OHCHR technical support
blocks.rationale: Suriname cooperates strategically with OHCHR, UNDP, UNICEF and other partners in capacity-strengthening.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 6 — Suriname: "the State cooperated strategically with international partners, including OHCHR, UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, IOM and PAHO, in support of capacity-strengthening and data validation"

recommendations.text: Request technical support from OHCHR to advance in the ratification of the main international human rights instruments to which the country is not yet a party, as well as to ensure the incorporation into its national legal system of the obligations deriving from ratified human rights treaties

blocks.summary: Sign the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action
blocks.rationale: The documents contain no information on this recommendation.

recommendations.text: Sign the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action and ratify the Convention on Cluster Munitions and the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons

blocks.summary: Ratify the Genocide Convention
blocks.rationale: A civil-society submission recommends ratification; none is reported.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/3), para. 6 — CGNK: "recommended that Suriname ratify the Convention on the Prevention and the Punishment of the crime of Genocide"

recommendations.text: Ratify the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide

blocks.summary: Establish and operationalise a national human rights institution
blocks.rationale: The draft National Human Rights Institute Act is still in pre-parliamentary consultation, with an intended completion date of November 2026; no institution exists.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 7 — Suriname: "The draft National Human Rights Institute Act is in the final pre-parliamentary consultation phase, with an intended completion date of end November 2026"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/3), para. 9 — JS6: "Suriname had persistently failed to establish and operationalize an independent national human rights institution"

recommendations.text: Establish and operationalize a national human rights institution in accordance with the Paris Principles (Chile); Establish and operationalize, in consultation with stakeholders, in particular with human rights civil society organizations, a national human rights institution in conformity with the Paris Principles (Haiti); Step up efforts to establish and operationalize a national human rights institution as per the Paris Principles (Nepal); Establish and operationalize a national human rights institution in accordance with the Paris Principles (Ukraine); Establish and fully operationalize a national human rights institution in accordance with the Paris Principles (Australia); Create a national human rights institution in accordance with the Paris Principles
Consider operationalization of the National Human Rights Institute in accordance with the Paris Principles
Continue the progress to establish and operationalize a national human rights institution in accordance with the Paris Principles, involving also possible bilateral and international cooperation
Intensify efforts to operationalize the work of the National Human Rights Institute in line with the Paris Principles
Advance the goal to establish a national human rights institution in accordance with the Paris Principles
Take steps to operationalize the National Human Rights Institute
Make further efforts to fully operationalize the National Human Rights Institute in accordance with the Paris Principles

Take dedicated measures to effectively operationalize the National Human Rights Institute, established in 2016, in compliance with the Paris Principles, with a broad mandate, including the promotion and protection of women’s rights, children’s rights and gender equality
Operationalize the National Human Rights Institute by allocating sufficient human, technical and financial resources in the national budget

themes.theme: Cooperation & Follow up with Special Procedures

blocks.summary: Extend a standing invitation to special procedures
blocks.rationale: No standing invitation has been extended; the UN country team recommends considering one.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 10 — United Nations country team: "recommended that Suriname consider issuing a standing invitation to the special procedure mandate holders"

recommendations.text: Extend a standing invitation to the special procedures of the Human Rights Council to ensure greater coordination and guarantee cooperation with the system
Consider the possibility of extending an open and standing invitation to all human rights mechanisms, as previously recommended
Issue a standing invitation to Human Rights Council special procedure mandate holders
Extend a standing invitation to the special procedures of the Human Rights Council
Extend a standing invitation to all special procedures of the Human Rights Council

blocks.summary: Establish a national mechanism for implementation, reporting and follow-up
blocks.rationale: The Human Rights Bureau of the Ministry of Justice and Police coordinates reporting with ministry focal points and a National Recommendations Tracking Database.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 10 — Suriname: "take place under the central direction of the Human Rights Bureau of the Ministry of Justice and Police"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 11 — Suriname: "the National Recommendations Tracking Database (NRTD)"

recommendations.text: Establish a permanent national mechanism for the implementation, reporting and follow-up of human rights recommendations, considering the possibility of receiving cooperation to that end within the framework of Sustainable Development Goals 16 and 17
Establish a national mechanism for implementation, reporting and follow-up of recommendations emanating from human rights bodies and mechanisms

blocks.summary: Legislate against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity
blocks.rationale: No such legislation exists; the 2023 LGBTQ+ Needs Assessment only identified priorities.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 27 — Suriname: "The Suriname LGBTQ+ Needs Assessment Report (2023) contributed to identifying priorities on inclusion and nondiscrimination"

recommendations.text: Take the necessary steps towards the adoption of legislative and other measures to explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity
Enact legislation that specifically addresses discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons
Consider passing legislation that specifically addresses discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity
Enact legislation to explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity

blocks.summary: Strengthen non-discrimination legislation
blocks.rationale: The Equal Treatment in Employment Act (2022) and the Act on Violence and Sexual Harassment in Employment (2022) were adopted; there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and no legislation on sexual orientation or gender identity.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 26 — Suriname: "Suriname has strengthened the legal framework on non-discrimination in the labour market"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 12 — Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination: "prioritize the drafting and adoption of a comprehensive anti-discrimination law"

recommendations.text: Pursue the efforts made previously in terms of the promotion of human rights and the protection of fundamental freedoms, particularly with regard to equality and non-discrimination

blocks.summary: Strengthen social protection and combat poverty
blocks.rationale: The National Social Protection Strategy 2024-2030, the Moni Karta cash-transfer system and a Multisectoral Early Childhood Development Policy 2025-2035 were adopted; multidimensional poverty remains widespread.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 85 — Suriname: "the National Social Protection Strategy (NSPS) 2024–2030"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 86 — Suriname: "In 2024, cash transfers reached 133,560 beneficiaries"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/3), para. 37 — JS6: "multidimensional poverty in Suriname affected up to 73% of large households"

recommendations.text: Continue to promote sustainable economic and social development, increase efforts to reduce poverty and improve people’s living standards
Further strengthen the social protection system and better protect the rights of persons in vulnerable situations
Continue to strengthen its successful national policies for the eradication of poverty and social exclusion
Continue taking steps to mitigate poverty and reduce socioeconomic impacts, and implement a national social security system

blocks.summary: National plan against child poverty
blocks.rationale: A General Child Allowance supports about 96,500 children and a Multisectoral Early Childhood Development Policy 2025-2035 was adopted.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 86 — Suriname: "the General Child Allowance supports approximately 96,500 children"

recommendations.text: Formulate public policies and a national plan to combat child poverty

blocks.summary: Implement the Nairobi Summit commitments
blocks.rationale: The SRHR Policy 2020-2030 and perinatal reforms implement the commitments.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 27 — Suriname: "the SRHR Policy 2020–2030 are being implemented"

recommendations.text: Implement the commitment made at the Nairobi Summit on the occasion of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the International Conference on Population and Development to put in place evidence-based population policies that promote sustainable development, equality and respect for human rights

blocks.summary: Make article 80 of the Civil Code gender neutral
blocks.rationale: The documents contain no information on this recommendation.

recommendations.text: Make article 80 of the Civil Code gender neutral to guarantee the full enjoyment of the right to family life by LGBTI+ persons

blocks.summary: Support the family through social policies
blocks.rationale: The new Civil Code (in force May 2025) strengthened the legal position of families and children.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 87 — Suriname: "The legal position of citizens and families has been further strengthened by the new Civil Code (S.B. 2024 no. 164), in force since 1 May 2025"

recommendations.text: Support, through economic and social policies, the institution of the family and the preservation of family values

blocks.summary: Climate adaptation and participation
blocks.rationale: Suriname implements its National Adaptation Plan 2020-2030 and updated NDCs.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 108 — Suriname: "Climate and adaptation policy is anchored in the National Adaptation Plan (NAP 2020–2030)"

recommendations.text: Ensure the meaningful participation of women, children, persons with disabilities and local communities in the development and implementation of climate change and disaster risk reduction frameworks
Take concrete and sustainable measures to fight against the negative effects of climate change
Continue to adopt an inclusive and participatory approach in climate adaptation initiatives

themes.theme: Rights related to name, identity & nationality

blocks.summary: Review gender identity policies
blocks.rationale: The documents contain no information on this recommendation.

recommendations.text: Review and make compatible with applicable law all policies and measures on gender recording in the deeds of the civil registry, to allow supplementing the registers of birth following gender and sex reassignment

blocks.summary: Abolish the death penalty
blocks.rationale: The death penalty was abolished in the Penal Code (2015) and in the Military Criminal Code (2021); the Second Optional Protocol remains unratified.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 7 — Suriname: "the amendment of the Military Criminal Code (S.B. 2021 no. 117), by which the death penalty was abolished"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 5 — United Nations country team: "Suriname had abolished the death penalty in the Penal Code in 2015 and in the Military Penal Code in 2021"

recommendations.text: Continue its efforts towards the complete abolition of the death penalty, with the abolition of the death penalty in its Military Penal Code
Abolish the use of death penalty and as a first step immediately establish an official moratorium on executions
Fully abolish the death penalty
Advance in the abolition of the death penalty in the Military Penal Code
Abolish the death penalty

blocks.summary: Abolish the death penalty in the Military Penal Code and ratify the Second Optional Protocol
blocks.rationale: The Military Criminal Code was amended in 2021 to abolish the death penalty, but the Second Optional Protocol remains unratified.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 7 — Suriname: "the amendment of the Military Criminal Code (S.B. 2021 no. 117), by which the death penalty was abolished"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 5 — United Nations country team: "ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty, remained pending"

recommendations.text: Step up efforts to abolish the death penalty through the revision of the Military Penal Code and consolidate this commitment through the prompt ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty

blocks.summary: Improve prison and detention conditions
blocks.rationale: The Penitentiary Institutions and Remand Centres Act and Decree (2023), a Central Resocialization Department (2025), new case managers and a forensic observation facility improve conditions; international bodies still call for improvements, notably at Santa Boma prison.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 42 — Suriname: "the Penitentiary Institutions and Remand Centres Act (S.B. 2023 no. 147) and the Penitentiary Decree (S.B. 2023 no. 148)"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 29 — Working Group of Experts on People of African Descent: "enhance its efforts to improve the conditions in places of deprivation of liberty"

recommendations.text: Take steps to modernize Surinamese prisons to an acceptable standard of safety, capacity and sanitation
Bring its prison and detention conditions fully into line with international human rights norms and standards, including the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners
Adopt comprehensive public policies aimed at ensuring the rights of persons deprived of liberty

themes.theme: Prohibition of torture & ill-treatment (including cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment)

blocks.summary: Investigate police ill-treatment and excessive force
blocks.rationale: Training on public-order maintenance and community-oriented policing was introduced and the police Personnel Investigation Department oversees use of force; civil society reports no prosecutions and calls for an independent oversight body.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 38 — Suriname: "Since 2025, the KPS has systematically moved to a community-oriented policing approach"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/3), para. 13 — JS6: "recommended that Suriname establish an independent oversight mechanism to investigate allegations of police misconduct"

recommendations.text: Investigate allegations of excessive force used by police and hold those responsible accountable

recommendations.by: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
recommendations.text: Enact comprehensive measures to address concerns of mistreatment by police, including the use of unnecessary force during arrests and beatings while in detention, this includes stopping the police from using violence or committing demeaning acts on persons found violating government curfew orders
Investigate reports of mistreatment by police, including the use of excessive force during arrests and beatings while in detention, and hold accountable any officers responsible

themes.theme: Human trafficking & contemporary forms of slavery

blocks.summary: Prevent and combat human trafficking
blocks.rationale: A National Action Plan on Human Trafficking (2021-2025), a specialised police TIP unit and a strengthened National Referral Mechanism are in place and Suriname is Tier 1; convictions remain low.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 53 — Suriname: "supported by the National Action Plan on Human Trafficking (2021–2025)"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 55 — Suriname: "the National Referral Mechanism was further strengthened for the identification, referral and protection of victims of human trafficking"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/3), para. 26 — ECLJ: "the number of convictions remained low"

recommendations.text: Redouble efforts to combat human trafficking in the framework of Sustainable Development Goals 5 and 16
Sustain the endeavours to prevent and combat human trafficking and guarantee assistance to the victims
Build the capacity of officials to improve identification and protection of victims of human trafficking
Continue efforts to combat trafficking in persons, in accordance with the requirements of the national action plan to prevent and combat trafficking in persons

recommendations.by: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
recommendations.text: Enforce legislation and provide adequate resources and training for all officials in the criminal justice system to effectively investigate and prosecute modern slavery cases
Intensify its efforts to combat child trafficking and sexual exploitation

blocks.summary: Shelters for victims of gender-based violence
blocks.rationale: The documents report insufficient shelter capacity and no new shelters; the State does not describe measures on shelters.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/3), para. 70 — JS6: "existing capacity was insufficient, with victims regularly being turned away"

recommendations.text: Take additional steps to prevent and combat trafficking in persons, such as creating specific shelters for victims, with a particular focus on women and girls from Amerindian and Maroon communities

blocks.summary: Prosecute traffickers more effectively
blocks.rationale: Convictions remain low.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 44 — Human Rights Committee: "the low number of convictions for trafficking in persons"

recommendations.text: Enforce the Penal Code more effectively to investigate and prosecute individuals and organized groups engaged in trafficking people for sexual and labour exploitation, with the maximum penalty of life imprisonment being sought in courts for egregious cases

blocks.summary: Reduce maternal mortality and expand sexual and reproductive health services
blocks.rationale: Suriname introduced the SIP Plus perinatal information system (2024-2025), the Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance model, the SRHR Policy 2020-2030 and has integrated comprehensive sexuality education into the curriculum; maternal mortality remains high.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 82 — Suriname: "The introduction and nationwide scaling-up of the SIP Plus perinatal information system in 2024 and 2025"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/3), para. 46 — JS6: "Suriname had reduced maternal mortality over time, but the level remained high"

recommendations.text: Advance in the development and implementation of measures to guarantee access to education and medical services in the field of sexual and reproductive health appropriate for each age group
Provide access to comprehensive sexuality education as part of the school curriculum
Develop a comprehensive sexual and reproductive health education programme, focusing on the prevention of adolescent pregnancies and sexually transmitted diseases

Advance in the implementation of measures to reduce the number of preventable maternal deaths by guaranteeing high-quality obstetric and postpartum care in health centres and universal access to care, especially for vulnerable women
Strengthen its efforts against maternal mortality, develop maternal health-care policies and measures that ensure accessible care for all women
Strengthen efforts to reduce the rate of maternal mortality
Provide access to safe and affordable contraceptives, family planning services and adequate information on sexual and reproductive health

blocks.summary: Decriminalise abortion
blocks.rationale: The documents contain no information on abortion.

recommendations.text: Decriminalize abortion by revising article 309 of the Penal Code to respect, protect and fulfil women’s and girls’ human rights to health

Decriminalize abortion in all circumstances and remove legal, administrative and practical barriers to accessing safe and legal abortion services in order to comply, inter alia, with article 36 (2) of the Constitution of Suriname

blocks.summary: Disability inclusion legislation and inclusive education
blocks.rationale: The General Act for Persons with Disabilities was introduced in the National Assembly (June 2024), a National Policy Plan 2025-2030 was adopted and an inclusive education protocol issued; accessibility barriers persist.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 66 — Suriname: "the formal member’s bill for the General Act for Persons with Disabilities (AWMB) was submitted to the National Assembly"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 67 — Suriname: "the National Policy Plan for Persons with Disabilities Suriname 2025–2030"

recommendations.text: Implement specific measures to promote inclusive education of children with disabilities
Enact a law to prohibit discrimination against persons with physical or mental disabilities in education, services or employment, and provide equal access to buildings (United States of America).

blocks.summary: Improve access to quality education, especially in the interior
blocks.rationale: Suriname adopted the National Education Policy Plan 2024-2031, a Multilingual Education Programme 2025-2030, school feeding, subsidised transport and a 2025 inclusive education protocol; dropout in the interior averages 21% and teacher and infrastructure gaps persist.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 71 — Suriname: "the National Education Policy Plan Suriname 2024–2031 (NOBS)"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 75 — Suriname: "the de facto school dropout in the interior, which averages 21 per cent"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 61 — United Nations country team: "Access to quality education remained limited, especially in the rainforest and for marginalized communities and children with disabilities"

recommendations.text: Adopt a coherent strategy to ensure universal access to education, especially in respect of girls, to reduce disparities in the level of education between rural and urban areas
Further intensify efforts towards the improvement of access to education for all children
Continue with legislative and policy measures for ensuring access to education for all children
Improve access to primary and secondary education for all children, including those with disabilities
Continue to allocate sufficient funding to ensure universal access to education, especially for children in the rural areas

Seek to improve access to primary and secondary education for all children, including those with disabilities

blocks.summary: Multilingual approach to education
blocks.rationale: The Multilingual Education Program 2025-2030 was ratified in 2024 and piloted in Galibi; scale-up faces barriers.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 74 — Suriname: "the Multilingual Education Program 2025–2030 was formally ratified in October 2024"

recommendations.text: Take appropriate measures towards the inclusion of a multilingual approach to education in the framework of Sustainable Development Goals 5 and 10

blocks.summary: Expand water, sanitation and hygiene programmes
blocks.rationale: UN WASH installed 118 rainwater tanks in 57 villages and a project for 26 rural communities is being implemented; less than 40% of people in the interior have safe drinking water.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 109 — Suriname: "the installation of automated surface-water treatment systems and 118 rainwater tanks in 57 villages has been realized through the UN WASH programs"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 109 — Suriname: "currently less than 40% of the population in the interior has structural access to safe drinking water"

recommendations.text: Expand the water, sanitation and hygiene programme to ensure access to improved water sources and sanitation facilities, especially for people living in the interior

blocks.summary: Eliminate violence against women

themes.theme: Labour rights and right to work

blocks.summary: Deepen measures for an adequate standard of living and decent work
blocks.rationale: The Decent Work Country Programme 2023-2026 and a revised Labour Act (2023) were implemented.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 88 — Suriname: "The Decent Work Country Program (DWCP) 2023–2026 promotes employment"

recommendations.text: Deepen measures to ensure the enjoyment of the right to an adequate standard of living by promoting decent work

blocks.summary: Improve access to essential health services and mental health
blocks.rationale: The Healthcare Facilities Readiness Initiative (June 2026), the Medical Mission for the interior, malaria-free certification (2025) and the National Mental Health Strategy 2025-2030 advance access; rural access, workforce and referral gaps remain.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 79 — Suriname: "on 25 June 2026 the State launched the large-scale Healthcare Facilities Readiness Initiative"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 80 — Suriname: "in 2025 the country was officially certified malaria-free by the World Health Organization"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 57 — UNICEF: "access to primary healthcare in remote areas was undermined by shortages of medical personnel"

recommendations.text: Consider further measures to ensure access to essential health services for all
Continue efforts in improving health-care infrastructure, in particular access to health care for women in rural communities
Continue the implementation of provisions under the national mental health plan to prevent suicides among children and adolescents
Strengthen efforts to ensure adequate provision of prenatal and postnatal care to address the rates of infant, child and maternal mortality

blocks.summary: Combat gender-based and domestic violence
blocks.rationale: Suriname adopted the Act on Violence and Sexual Harassment in Employment (2022), implements the Gender Vision Policy 2021-2035, trains first responders and opened a specialised victim hearing room (March 2026); implementation of the 2009 Domestic Violence Act is weak, shelter capacity is insufficient and the 2022 Act excludes public servants.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 26 — Suriname: "the Equal Treatment in Employment Act (S.B. 2022 no. 137) and the Act on Violence and Sexual Harassment in Employment (S.B. 2022 no. 136)"

National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 45 — Suriname: "a specialized hearing room was put into operation at the De Nieuwe Grond police station for the reception and questioning of victims of domestic and gender-based violence"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 73 — Human Rights Committee: "regretted the reportedly weak implementation of its legislative framework"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/3), para. 70 — JS6: "existing capacity was insufficient, with victims regularly being turned away"

recommendations.text: Implement the law on domestic violence more efficiently and provide adequate protection for victims of domestic violence, inter alia, by efficiently holding perpetrators accountable and giving victims adequate legal and psychosocial support
Implement a multisectoral policy approach, aiming at enhancing and guaranteeing the provision of professional gender-based violence services, especially in rural areas
Continue taking measures to eradicate all forms of violence and discrimination against women, girls and lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons
Strengthen the efforts to combat all forms of violence and discrimination against women and girls, children and lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons
Diversify national plans to strengthen gender equality policies and the fight against gender-based violence in the country
Continue to strengthen its programmes for the empowerment of women and gender equality, especially in the area of the fight against domestic violence
Take adequate measures to protect women and children from domestic violence
Ensure greater stakeholder involvement in developing and implementing measures to prevent and address all forms of gender-based violence
Enhance the progress made in combating domestic violence, especially against women, preventing discrimination against women and supporting gender equality in various fields
Continue to address domestic violence and promote efforts to combat all forms of violence against women and girls

blocks.summary: Shelters for victims of gender-based violence
blocks.rationale: The documents report insufficient shelter capacity and no new shelters; the State does not describe measures on shelters.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/3), para. 70 — JS6: "existing capacity was insufficient, with victims regularly being turned away"

recommendations.text: Establish additional shelters for victims of gender-based violence, especially in rural areas, and ensure that legal assistance, rehabilitation and psychosocial support are provided to victims there
Actively encourage use of and access to shelters for survivors of gender-based violence, as well as expand educational and outreach programmes to encourage survivors to report abuse

Continue its endeavours to combat gender-based violence, including domestic violence, and ensure that shelters and health-care services are accessible to all victims, especially to those from rural backgrounds

blocks.summary: Legislate against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity
blocks.rationale: No such legislation exists; the 2023 LGBTQ+ Needs Assessment only identified priorities.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 27 — Suriname: "The Suriname LGBTQ+ Needs Assessment Report (2023) contributed to identifying priorities on inclusion and nondiscrimination"

recommendations.by: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
recommendations.text: Seek training for law enforcement and judicial officers to ensure accountability for gender-based violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex communities

blocks.summary: Strengthen child-protection systems and legislation
blocks.rationale: The Children's Ombudsperson Act (2025), the lowering of the age of majority to 18 and equal status for all children in the new Civil Code advance child protection; the Ombudsman institute is not yet operational and corporal punishment is not prohibited in all settings.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 60 — Suriname: "provides for the establishment of the Children’s Ombudsman Institute Suriname (KOI)"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 18 — United Nations country team: "it was not yet operational, its bureau had not been staffed"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 61 — Suriname: "the statutory age of majority has been lowered de jure from 21 to 18 years"

recommendations.text: Adopt measures to eliminate all forms of discrimination and violence against children, with special attention to Amerindian and Maroon communities, migrants and children of Haitian migrants

Continue to strengthen its child protection systems, including by further implementing its integrated child protection network and considering establishing specialized courts and police units for child protection
Strengthen ongoing actions for the protection of children’s rights, including actions in the legislative sphere
Continue effective measures to protect the rights of the child, including by eradicating child labour, child abuse and reducing school dropout rates
Step up efforts for child protection by adopting regulatory instruments and policies and by providing the IKBeN network with adequate resources and assistance

blocks.summary: Prohibit corporal punishment in all settings
blocks.rationale: The State describes elimination of corporal punishment in education only; the Human Rights Committee requests that parents' corporal punishment also be prohibited in the Civil Code.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 85 — Human Rights Committee: "prohibiting corporal punishment by parents in the draft New Civil Code"

recommendations.text: Bolster measures that would provide for a complete prohibition of corporal punishment against boys and girls

Amend legislation to explicitly prohibit corporal punishment in all settings, including in the family, in day-care and afterschool care facilities, schools, alternative care settings and residential care
Abolish corporal punishment, in law and in practice, by enacting specific national legislation prohibiting corporal punishment in all environments

blocks.summary: Eliminate child, early and forced marriage
blocks.rationale: UNESCO requests that the minimum age of marriage be 18 without exception; the State only states that customary law cannot override national law.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 87 — UNESCO: "amend its legislation to ensure that the minimum age of marriage was 18 years old without exception"

recommendations.text: Continue efforts in eliminating child, early and forced marriages, as well as sexual abuse and exploitation of children, especially girls

themes.theme: Persons with disabilities: definition, general principles

blocks.summary: Comprehensive legislation to protect persons with disabilities
blocks.rationale: The General Act for Persons with Disabilities is before the National Assembly.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 66 — Suriname: "the formal member’s bill for the General Act for Persons with Disabilities (AWMB) was submitted to the National Assembly"

recommendations.text: Consider adopting comprehensive legislation to protect the rights of persons with disabilities

blocks.summary: Promote gender equality and women's participation
blocks.rationale: The Gender Vision Policy Document 2021-2035 guides training of first responders and officials; negative gender stereotypes and low representation persist.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 27 — Suriname: "the Gender Vision Policy Document 2021–2035 and the SRHR Policy 2020–2030 are being implemented"

recommendations.text: Continue advancing in the fight against gender stereotypes and prejudices, and for the achievement of gender equality
Take necessary measures to achieve gender equality in political and public life

Advance efforts to raise awareness regarding equal opportunities and responsibilities for men and women in order to abolish discrimination on the basis of gender and encourage greater representation of women in positions of responsibility

blocks.summary: Adopt legislation on equal treatment of women and men
blocks.rationale: The Equal Treatment in Employment Act (2022) was adopted; the ILO continues to call for comprehensive legislation covering all grounds.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 48 — ILO Committee of Experts: "reiterated its request to Suriname to adopt as soon as possible comprehensive legislation that"

recommendations.text: Adopt the draft law on equal treatment of women and men and ensure it includes a definition of discrimination against women in line with article 1 of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women

blocks.summary: Protect children from economic exploitation
blocks.rationale: The Youth Information Unit runs prevention programmes and the Labour Act was revised in 2023.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 64 — Suriname: "the Youth Information Unit of the Suriname Police Force continuously carries out prevention and awareness programs"

recommendations.text: Take measures to protect children from being economically exploited and adopt policies to effectively address child labour in both the formal and informal sectors

blocks.summary: Eradicate child labour
blocks.rationale: The ILO continues to request measures including on hazardous work in mining.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 84 — ILO Committee of Experts: "to ensure that no child was engaged in hazardous work in mining"

recommendations.text: Eradicate child labour

themes.theme: Right to an adequate standard of living

blocks.summary: Recognise Indigenous and tribal peoples' rights
blocks.rationale: Suriname launched a Land Rights Project 2026-2030 with UNDP, received a national FPIC protocol (October 2025) and the National Assembly approved the Act on the Protection of Residential and Living Areas of Indigenous and Tribal Peoples; the Collective Rights Act is still a draft.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 96 — Suriname: "the Act on the Protection of the Residential and Living Areas of Indigenous and Tribal Peoples has been approved by the National Assembly"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 95 — Suriname: "formally handed over the national FPIC protocol to the Government on 14 October 2025"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 96 — Human Rights Committee: "to expedite the adoption, within a clear time frame, of the draft law on the collective rights of Indigenous and tribal peoples"

recommendations.text: Increase efforts to recognize indigenous peoples and demarcate their traditional territories through legislation

Continue to boost the changes in the regulatory and the institutional framework for the promotion and protection of human rights that would lead to greater inclusion and better standards of living for indigenous peoples and communities
Adopt measures to strengthen the effective exercise of the economic rights of indigenous peoples and their special protection
Step up the process of legal and formal recognition of indigenous and tribal peoples in order to improve their situation and guarantee their rights

blocks.summary: Mitigate mercury and mining pollution
blocks.rationale: The National Environmental Authority is operational and Suriname implements the Minamata Convention through a 2021-2025 action plan for small-scale gold mining; contamination persists in the interior.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 108 — Suriname: "Suriname implements the Minamata Convention on Mercury through the NAP-ASGM (2021–2025)"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 69 — Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination: "reports of ongoing pollution – mercury and other toxics – on land and in rivers"

recommendations.text: Take actions, in follow-up to the recommendations of the second cycle, on mitigating the negative impact of mining to strengthen the legal framework for the rights of indigenous populations, respecting the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment

themes.theme: Right to participate in public affairs & right to vote

blocks.summary: Meaningful participation of Indigenous peoples
blocks.rationale: A national FPIC protocol was handed over and consultations were held.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 95 — Suriname: "formally handed over the national FPIC protocol to the Government on 14 October 2025"

recommendations.text: Take further steps to ensure the meaningful participation of indigenous peoples in decision-making on all matters affecting them

blocks.summary: Platform to protect the rights of Indigenous and tribal peoples
blocks.rationale: Consultations with traditional authorities, the FPIC protocol and an inter-ministerial commission were launched.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 95 — Suriname: "an interministerial commission is currently studying modalities to integrate this protocol as a formal guideline for consultations in the interior"

recommendations.text: Establish a formal platform to guarantee and protect the rights of indigenous and tribal peoples

blocks.summary: Implement the judgments of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights
blocks.rationale: Suriname recognises remaining constitutional challenges in implementing the Moiwana, Saramaka and Kaliña and Lokono judgments; the Human Rights Committee finds them only partially implemented.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 7 — Suriname: "recognizes the remaining constitutional challenges in the full de jure implementation of the standing judgments of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/2), para. 11 — Human Rights Committee: "had been only partially implemented"

recommendations.text: Implement the judgment of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights regarding the Moiwana Community and Saramaka people swiftly and completely
Ensure full and swift implementation of the various judgments made by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights regarding the land rights of indigenous peoples in Suriname

blocks.summary: Enact a law to demarcate Indigenous lands
blocks.rationale: The Collective Rights Act is still before the National Assembly; the Act on the Protection of Residential and Living Areas was approved pending promulgation and a Land Rights Project was launched.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SUR/1), para. 94 — Suriname: "the draft Act on the Collective Rights of Indigenous and Tribal Peoples (initiated in 2019, with renewed parliamentary treatment in 2023–2025)"

recommendations.text: Enact a law that provides for demarcation of the lands of indigenous peoples and empowerment regarding decisions affecting the exploitation of natural resources on their lands (United States of America).

meta.caveat: The Human Rights Committee's follow-up procedure grades only the two to four “priority” recommendations it selected from this country's Concluding Observations (CoBs). The other CoBs are not graded.

paragraphs.title: National human rights institution
paragraphs.recommendation: The State party should take measures to ensure the effective functioning of the National Human Rights Institute with a broad human rights mandate, and provide it with adequate financial and human resources, in line with the principles relating to the status of national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights (the Paris Principles)

limbs.eval: The Committee welcomes the launch of the National Human Rights Institute in 2016, and requires additional information on the planned measures aimed at ensuring its compliance with the Paris Principles, the progress in the implementation of those measures and the anticipated time frame for achieving the Institute’s full compliance with the Principles, including with regard to institutional and financial independence and autonomy, and its mandate

paragraphs.title: Impunity for past human rights violations
paragraphs.recommendation: Recalling its previous recommendation (see CCPR/CO/80/SUR, para. 7), the Committee urges the State party to repeal the Amnesty Act. The State party should also comply forthwith with international human rights law requiring accountability for those responsible for serious human rights violations in respect of which States are required to bring perpetrators to justice, including by completing the pending criminal prosecutions. In this regard, the Committee draws attention to its general comment No. 31 (2004) on the nature of the general legal obligation imposed on States parties to the Covenant, in particular paragraph 18, in which the Committee states that States parties may not relieve perpetrators of acts such as torture, arbitrary or extrajudicial killings or enforced disappearance from their personal responsibility. The State party should also ensure the effective protection of witnesses and diligently enquire into all cases of suspected witness intimidation

limbs.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
limbs.eval: The Committee regrets that the State party does not intend to repeal the Amnesty Act and that no measures have been taken to bring perpetrators of serious human rights violations, including for the Moiwana massacre of 1986, to justice, including by completing the pending criminal prosecutions brought against the President, Desiré Bouterse, and 24 others accused of the extrajudicial executions of 15 political opponents in December 1982. The Committee reiterates its recommendation, and recalls its general comment No. 31 (2004) on the nature of the general legal obligation imposed on States parties to the Covenant, in particular paragraph 18, in which it indicates that States parties may not relieve perpetrators of acts such as torture, arbitrary or extrajudicial killings or enforced disappearance from personal responsibility. The Committee regrets the State party’s assertion that it has no knowledge of cases of threats or harm to witnesses, and requests information on progress made in securing witness testimonies in relation to the Moiwana case and on any witness protection measures and programmes in place to ensure the effective protection of witnesses against any kind of intimidation or threats

paragraphs.title: Judicial control of detention
paragraphs.recommendation: The State party should adopt legislation to ensure that anyone arrested or detained on a criminal charge is brought before a judge within 48 hours. The Committee draws the attention of the State party to its general comment No. 35 (2014) on liberty and security of person, in particular paragraph 33, in which it states that 48 hours is ordinarily sufficient to transport the individual and to prepare for the judicial hearing. An especially strict standard of promptness, such as 24 hours, should apply in the case of juveniles. Moreover, a public prosecutor cannot be considered an officer exercising judicial power under article 9 (3) of the Covenant (see para. 32 of the general comment)

limbs.eval: The Committee regrets that the State party has not adopted legislation requiring that anyone arrested or detained on a criminal charge be brought before a judge within 48 hours, invoking resource constraints. It notes the stated intention of the State party to do everything in its power to ensure the implementation of the recommendation. The Committee requires clarification as to whether the judicial control of detention under article 9 (3) of the Covenant is exercised by a public prosecutor or by a judge. The Committee reiterates its recommendation
